query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

There has been a notable increase of interest in the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last years due to their outstanding properties, e.g., excellent strength and fracture toughness, high hardness, good wear and corrosion resistance, and good thermal conductivity. The HEAs contain several elements in equimolar or near equimolar ratios that often possess different ground state crystal structures. However, the majority of these reported alloys exhibit two simple structures, i.e., face-centered cubic (fcc) or body-centered cubic (bcc), whereas only few single-phase HEAs with hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure have been produced. Among those, the hcp HEAs containing rare earth elements did not show compositional segregation, e.g., DyGdHoTbY, but they typically lacked pronounced solid-solution hardening due to the similar size and electronic structure of the constituents. Attempts to synthesize single-phase hcp HEAs without rare earth elements have been rare until now owing to compositional segregation.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a great deal of attention in recent years due to their excellent mechanical properties, such as good ductility, superior fatigue properties, and high strength, thermal stability, and wear resistance. The name refers to the new design philosophy of alloying by introducing more metal elements. The most well-known HEA is the equimolar ratio CoCrFeNiMn alloy, also known as the Cantor alloy,. Although it has a complicated chemical composition, it forms a simple solid solution phase that gives it extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness at elevated temperatures (approximately 900 °C). The yield strength and tensile strength of CoCrFeNiMn, however, is relatively low, and this imbalanced mechanical performance limits its potential applications. Therefore, it is crucial to improve its strength without introducing additional brittleness. The strength of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy is affected by the phase of its microstructures.
